title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 11–12 (reviewed)
description: Reviewed vocabulary and expressions from the kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, and everyday routines, including reference-page and exercise-based learning targets.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, labelled illustrations, dialogues, and exercises 11.1–11.4 and 12.1–12.6 were inspected. Teaching extensions are identified where applicable.

units.title: Unit 11 — In the kitchen
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 11, printed pages 28–29 (PDF pages 29–30); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: Our kitchen is small but bright.
items.note: A kitchen is the room where people prepare food and often eat meals.

items.example: Put the milk in the fridge.
items.note: Fridge is the common short form of refrigerator. It keeps food cold but does not freeze it.

items.example: The vegetables are in the freezer.
items.note: A freezer is colder than a fridge and keeps food frozen. A fridge and a freezer are not interchangeable.

items.example: I heat my lunch in the microwave.
items.note: A microwave is used to heat or cook food quickly; microwave oven is the longer name.

items.example: The cups are in the cupboard.
items.note: The letter p is silent: /ˈkʌbəd/. A cupboard is a storage space with a door, often attached to the wall.

items.example: The tea is on the top shelf.
items.note: The plural is shelves /ʃelvz/, not shelfs. Something can be on a shelf.

items.example: Turn on the tap for some water.
items.note: British English tap corresponds to faucet in American English. Turn on the tap to get water.

items.example: Leave the dishes in the sink.
items.note: A sink is a basin used mainly for washing dishes or food in a kitchen; compare bathroom basin.

items.example: Put the bowl on the worktop.
items.note: Worktop is common in British English; countertop is a common American English equivalent.

items.example: The bin is under the sink.
items.note: A bin is a container for rubbish. Rubbish bin is a common British English expression.

items.example: The washing machine is next to the sink.
items.note: A washing machine washes clothes. A dishwasher washes plates, cups and cutlery.

items.example: The soup is on the cooker.
items.note: A cooker is an appliance used for cooking, often with an oven and hobs. Cook can be a verb or a person.

items.example: We use the dishwasher every evening.
items.note: A dishwasher washes plates, glasses and cutlery; a washing machine washes clothes.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: The teapot is on the table.
items.note: A teapot holds tea for serving. A kettle is used to heat water; the two are different.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: She bought a new coffee maker.
items.note: A coffee maker is equipment for preparing coffee; several types exist.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: Heat the sauce in a saucepan.
items.note: A saucepan is a deep cooking pan, usually with a long handle, used on a cooker.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: We need more kitchen roll.
items.note: Kitchen roll is British English for a roll of absorbent paper used for cleaning and drying.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: Dry the plates with a tea towel.
items.note: A tea towel dries dishes and cutlery; despite its name, it is not for making tea.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: Use washing-up liquid to wash the plates.
items.note: Washing-up liquid is British English for liquid soap used to wash dishes by hand.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: Fry the eggs in a frying pan.
items.note: A frying pan is a shallow pan used for frying food; it is not a cup or drinking vessel.

items.section: B · Things we use in the kitchen
items.example: Clean the worktop with a cloth.
items.note: A cloth is a piece of fabric used for cleaning or drying. The plural is cloths /klɒθs/.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: I eat noodles with chopsticks.
items.note: Chopsticks are normally used as a plural noun for the two sticks used together to eat food.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: Can I have a glass of water?
items.note: A glass is a drinking container; glass can also refer to the material it is made from.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: Use a knife to cut the bread.
items.note: The initial k is silent. The plural is knives /naɪvz/, not knifes.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: The fork is next to the plate.
items.note: A fork is used to pick up or hold food when eating.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: Stir your coffee with a spoon.
items.note: A spoon is used to eat, serve or stir food and drink.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: Would you like a cup of tea?
items.note: A cup usually has a handle and may be smaller than a mug. Both can be used for hot drinks.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: There is rice in the bowl.
items.note: A bowl is a deep open container, for example for soup, cereal or rice.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: I drink coffee from a large mug.
items.note: A mug is often larger and taller than a cup; both are drinking containers.

items.section: C · Things for eating and drinking
items.example: Please put your plate on the table.
items.note: A plate is a flat dish for serving or eating food.

items.example: Where can I find a clean mug?
items.note: Ask Where can I find + an object? to ask about its location. Complete the question before speaking it aloud.
items.speechText: Where can I find a mug?

items.example: The glasses are in the cupboard.
items.note: Use in for something inside a cupboard or another enclosed space.

items.example: The cups are on the shelf.
items.note: Use on for something resting on a shelf or another surface.

items.example: Leave the pan on the worktop.
items.note: The preposition on describes an object resting on the worktop.

items.example: Turn on the tap to wash your hands.
items.note: Turn on the tap means open it so water can flow; this expression appears in the exercises.

items.example: Turn off the tap when you finish.
items.note: Turn off the tap means close it to stop the water; compare turn on the tap. This is a teaching extension.

items.example: Can you help with the washing-up?
items.note: Washing-up is British English for washing dishes by hand. Use help with + noun phrase.

items.example: Can I help with the cooking?
items.note: Use help with + noun or -ing noun phrase: Can I help with the cooking?

items.example: I'll wash and you can dry the plates.
items.note: Dry means remove water; it is different from wash. The expression appears in the dialogue.

items.example: We can cook some rice for dinner.
items.note: Rice is usually uncountable, so some rice is natural when the amount is not specified.

items.example: Where does this saucepan go?
items.note: Where does this + noun + go? asks where an object is normally kept, not where it is travelling.

items.example: Put it in the cupboard, please.
items.note: Use put + object + place: Put it in the cupboard. Put is the same in the present and past forms.

items.example: I wash the dishes after lunch.
items.note: Wash the dishes is a common alternative to do the washing-up; included as a teaching extension.

learningObjectives: Identify the main kitchen appliances, storage spaces and work areas shown in the unit.
Match utensils, dishes and cleaning supplies to preparing, serving and cleaning up after meals.
Ask where kitchen items can be found or put away, and offer help with cooking or washing-up.
Distinguish fridge from freezer, washing machine from dishwasher, and cup from mug.
Describe object locations using in, on, under and next to, as practised in the illustrations and exercises.

units.title: Unit 12 — In the bedroom and bathroom
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 12, printed pages 30–31 (PDF pages 31–32); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: The bed is near the window.
items.note: A bed is a piece of furniture used for sleeping. Compare go to bed, which does not take an article.

items.example: I read with my bedside lamp on.
items.note: A bedside lamp provides light near a bed, often for reading.

items.example: My alarm clock rings at seven.
items.note: An alarm clock makes a sound at a set time to wake someone up.

items.example: I put on my pyjamas before bed.
items.note: Pyjamas is the British spelling (US: pajamas). It normally takes a plural verb: My pyjamas are clean.

items.example: Her comb is on the dressing table.
items.note: A dressing table is a piece of bedroom furniture often used for grooming or putting on make-up.

items.example: There is a comb in the drawer.
items.note: The final b is silent: /kəʊm/. A comb is used to arrange or tidy hair.

items.example: My shirts are in the chest of drawers.
items.note: A chest of drawers contains several drawers used for keeping clothes or other things.

items.example: There is a mirror next to the wardrobe.
items.note: You look in a mirror to see your reflection.

items.example: My coats are in the wardrobe.
items.note: A wardrobe is a tall cupboard for storing clothes, especially hanging clothes.

items.example: My book is on the bedside table.
items.note: A bedside table is a small table next to the bed, often used for a lamp, clock or book.

items.example: I keep my hairbrush in the bedroom.
items.note: A hairbrush is used to brush hair; compare comb.

items.example: There is toothpaste by the basin.
items.note: Toothpaste is usually uncountable: some toothpaste, a tube of toothpaste.

items.example: Pack your toothbrush for the trip.
items.note: A toothbrush is used to clean teeth; the plural is toothbrushes.

items.example: The towels are on the bathroom shelf.
items.note: The plural is shelves /ʃelvz/. This item also appears in Unit 11 in a kitchen context.

items.example: Wash your hands with soap.
items.note: Soap is normally uncountable when it means the substance. You can say a bar of soap.

items.example: The basin is next to the shower.
items.note: A basin is a bathroom washbasin; sink is commonly used for the kitchen equivalent.

items.example: He bought a new razor.
items.note: A razor is used for shaving. A razor blade is a part of some kinds of razor.

items.example: The toilet is near the basin.
items.note: Toilet can refer to the fixture or, especially in British English, to the room containing it.

items.example: The shower is very hot.
items.note: Shower can mean the bathroom fixture or the act of washing under running water: have a shower.

items.example: We need more shampoo.
items.note: Shampoo is usually uncountable as a product for washing hair.

items.example: I use shower gel in the morning.
items.note: Shower gel is a liquid product used for washing the body in the shower.

items.example: There is a clean towel on the shelf.
items.note: A towel is used to dry your body or hands after washing.

items.example: I usually go to bed at ten.
items.note: Go to bed means start preparing to sleep or go to your bed; do not say go to the bed for this routine meaning.

items.pt: subir as escadas; ir para o andar de cima
items.example: She goes upstairs after dinner.
items.note: Upstairs can indicate movement to a higher floor or a position on a higher floor.

items.example: He gets undressed before a shower.
items.note: Get undressed means take your clothes off; compare get dressed.

items.example: I get into bed and open a book.
items.note: Get into bed describes physically entering the bed, usually before sleeping.

items.example: I read for a bit before sleeping.
items.note: For a bit means for a short time; the phrase is used for an activity before sleep.

items.example: Turn off the light before you sleep.
items.note: Turn off means stop a light or machine from working; compare turn on.

items.example: I often fall asleep quickly.
items.note: Fall asleep means begin sleeping. Be asleep describes the state of sleeping.

items.example: I wake up at half past six.
items.note: Wake up means stop sleeping. You may wake up before you get up.

items.example: My alarm clock rings every morning.
items.note: Ring describes the noise made by an alarm clock. The verb forms are ring, rang, rung.

items.example: I get up ten minutes after I wake up.
items.note: Get up means leave your bed after waking. It is different from wake up.

items.example: I have a shower before breakfast.
items.note: Have a shower is common in British English; take a shower is also common.

items.example: I clean my teeth twice a day.
items.note: Clean your teeth means brush them with a toothbrush; brush your teeth is also widely used.

items.example: She gets dressed after her shower.
items.note: Get dressed means put your clothes on; the opposite is get undressed.

items.pt: descer as escadas; ir para baixo
items.example: We go downstairs for breakfast.
items.note: Downstairs means towards or on a lower floor; compare go upstairs.

items.example: I have breakfast at eight.
items.note: Have breakfast means eat the morning meal. Normally there is no article before breakfast.

items.example: My night-time routine is simple.
items.note: A night-time routine is a usual sequence of activities before sleep; the expression occurs in exercise 12.6.

items.example: Her morning routine starts early.
items.note: A morning routine is the usual sequence of things someone does after waking; the expression occurs in exercise 12.6.

learningObjectives: Identify bedroom furniture and bathroom equipment shown in the illustrations.
Describe items and their positions in a bedroom or bathroom.
Describe the sequence of ordinary night-time and morning activities.
Distinguish wake up from get up, fall asleep from go to bed, and get dressed from get undressed.
Talk about basic personal hygiene and what to pack for an overnight visit.
